issues.item: Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed
issues.explanation: 'Feeling happy or relaxed' as a trigger is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only broad internal-state trigger alongside trauma-linked cues (hearing related names, ambulances) and is weakly connected to the rest of the formulation. The other nodes emphasize intrusive war memories, negative self-appraisals, and avoidance; a relaxation trigger without any corresponding threat content or appraisals about letting guard down is clinically hard to anchor here.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Mirror Checking: keep checking mirrors
issues.explanation: 'Keep checking mirrors' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. Mirror checking usually implies appearance/body-focused concern or hypervigilant scanning for current danger, but this profile has no Threat items and the formulation isolates Threat from the active network. The remaining maladaptive strategies (avoiding sleep, revenge fantasies) fit trauma intrusions and appraisals, whereas mirror checking addresses a symptom theme not otherwise represented.

vignette: Mr. Tran was 30 years old when he experienced the traumatic event that continues to haunt him nearly five decades later. Born in South Vietnam, he grew up during the height of the war and lived through countless air raids, bombings, and skirmishes. One fateful day, while he was working at a local factory, an explosion shook the entire region. The ground trembled, and shrapnel rained down on the area around him. Mr. Tran remembers the moment vividly: the blinding flash of light, the deafening roar that seemed to tear through his eardrums, and the acrid smell of smoke and burnt earth. The memory feels alien to him now, as if it belongs to someone else rather than himself. Yet, when he least expects it, the images force their way into his mind with startling clarity-details so vivid that they can feel like they are happening all over again. Mr. Tran often finds himself staring blankly at a wall or the floor, lost in those moments from decades ago. Mr. Tran's marriage to his wife of nearly 50 years has been his anchor throughout these years. However, even their relationship is affected by his constant need for vigilance. He constantly scans his surroundings, looking out for any signs that might indicate another threat. This hyper-vigilance often leaves him feeling drained and exhausted. As a firefighter, Mr. Tran's occupation places him in emergency contexts frequently. The sound of sirens from ambulances sends a wave of anxiety through him, triggering memories of the explosions he survived during the war. He tries to avoid these triggers by staying away from areas where emergencies are common, but his work requires him to be present at such scenes. Sleep has become a source of significant distress for Mr. Tran. The dark and quiet of the night often feel like they amplify his fears, making it difficult for him to rest peacefully. He often finds himself going through routines of checking doors and windows before he can finally lie down. Even then, the memories and thoughts are relentless, making sleep a constant battle. In moments when the memories overwhelm him, Mr. Tran imagines getting revenge on those responsible for the explosions. These fantasies offer temporary relief but only fuel his ongoing distress. He is certain that if he thinks about the event, he will not be able to handle it, and this thought alone makes him avoid confronting his emotions and experiences. Mr. Tran feels a deep sense of dehumanization; sometimes, he struggles with feeling like an object rather than a person. This sense of disconnection from himself exacerbates his feelings of isolation and despair. He often wonders if somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, further contributing to his negative self-appraisals. The cumulative effect of these symptoms has taken a toll on Mr. Tran's quality of life. His wife notices that he is increasingly withdrawn and avoids social gatherings. Their once close relationship has become strained as she struggles to understand the depth of his suffering. What finally brought Mr. Tran to seek help was a particularly severe episode where the memories forced themselves into his mind while he was on duty, causing him to freeze in place during an emergency response. The incident left him feeling exposed and vulnerable, and for the first time, he realized that his coping mechanisms were no longer sufficient. Mr. Tran is most afraid of losing control completely or becoming a burden to those around him. He hopes that therapy will help him manage his symptoms better and provide some sense of peace, allowing him to reclaim his life without being constantly haunted by the past.
